steps.tx: **Thiamine pyrophosphate**, TPP, is the active coenzyme form of vitamin B1. It carries activated aldehyde groups in four key reactions. Three are oxidative decarboxylations sharing the same machinery: pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase and branched chain ketoacid dehydrogenase. The fourth, transketolase, runs in the pentose phosphate pathway and is the basis of the laboratory test.
steps.say: TPP powers three big decarboxylation complexes plus transketolase. If you can name those four reactions, most thiamine questions fall into place.

steps.tx: **Tiny stores** make thiamine the first vitamin to run out. The body holds only about two to three weeks of supply, so alcohol use disorder, vomiting, dialysis and refeeding after starvation can empty reserves quickly. Historically, polished rice diets caused epidemics because milling removes the thiamine rich husk while leaving the starchy grain.
steps.say: You carry only a few weeks of thiamine. Alcohol, vomiting and refeeding drain it fast, and polished rice diets caused the classic epidemics.

steps.tx: **Beriberi patterns** split by system affected. Dry beriberi is a symmetrical ascending peripheral neuropathy with wasting and foot drop. Wet beriberi adds high output cardiac failure with oedema and breathlessness, because failing energy metabolism dilates vessels and the heart cannot keep up. Infantile beriberi strikes breastfed babies of deficient mothers and can kill quickly.
steps.say: Dry beriberi climbs the legs as neuropathy. Wet beriberi floods the lungs through high output heart failure, and the infant form can be rapidly fatal.

steps.tx: **Wernicke encephalopathy** is the emergency presentation. Confusion, ataxia and eye signs such as nystagmus and ophthalmoplegia form the classic triad, though all three rarely appear together. Lesions centre on the mammillary bodies and periaqueductal grey. Untreated, it progresses to Korsakoff syndrome, with severe memory loss and confabulation that seldom fully reverses.
steps.say: Confusion, unsteady gait and abnormal eye movements mean Wernicke until proved otherwise. Treat first, because the memory damage of Korsakoff syndrome is usually permanent.

steps.tx: **Glucose before thiamine** can precipitate collapse. A glucose load suddenly increases flux through pyruvate dehydrogenase, consuming the last available TPP and tipping a borderline brain into Wernicke. The safe sequence in any at risk patient is thiamine before, or at worst together with, intravenous glucose. This single ordering rule is asked repeatedly in examinations.
steps.say: Glucose burns through the last thiamine a borderline patient has. Always give thiamine before glucose in anyone at risk, never the other way round.

steps.tx: **Red cell transketolase** testing confirms deficiency. Because transketolase needs TPP, adding TPP to a red cell sample and measuring the activity rise estimates body stores; a large rise means the enzyme was sitting empty. In practice, clinicians treat on suspicion rather than wait, since thiamine is cheap, safe and time critical.
steps.say: The transketolase test shows whether the enzyme sits empty waiting for TPP. Clinically, though, suspicion alone is enough to treat immediately.
